<#
Proves the campaign budget guarantee holds under concurrent HTTP load.

Creates a campaign with budget=100, fires 2000 concurrent POST /impression/{id}
requests at it via `hey` (https://github.com/rakyll/hey), then checks GET /stats/{id}
to confirm exactly 100 impressions were accepted, spent==100, remaining==0, and the
campaign is paused.

The backend's port is NOT published in docker-compose, so:
  - Default -BaseUrl (http://localhost:8080) targets a locally-run backend, e.g.
    `go run ./cmd/server` from backend/.
  - To hit the docker-compose stack instead, go through nginx:
    -BaseUrl http://localhost:3000/api

To prove the guarantee holds across multiple backend instances sharing the same
database (the actual point of this test), scale the backend and re-run through
nginx:
    docker compose up -d --scale backend=2
    ./loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1 -BaseUrl http://localhost:3000/api

Requires `hey` on PATH (or pass -HeyPath): go install github.com/rakyll/hey@latest

Usage:
    ./loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1
    ./loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1 -BaseUrl http://localhost:3000/api
#>

param(
    [string]$BaseUrl = "http://localhost:8080",
    [string]$HeyPath = "hey"
)

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$BaseUrl = $BaseUrl.TrimEnd("/")

if (-not (Get-Command $HeyPath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    Write-Host "ERROR: '$HeyPath' not found on PATH." -ForegroundColor Red
    Write-Host "Install it with: go install github.com/rakyll/hey@latest"
    exit 1
}

# --- Create campaign -------------------------------------------------------

$startDate = [DateTime]::UtcNow
$endDate = $startDate.AddDays(1)
$dateFormat = "yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ"

$createBody = @{
    title      = "loadtest-$($startDate.ToString('yyyyMMddHHmmss'))"
    budget     = 100
    start_date = $startDate.ToString($dateFormat)
    end_date   = $endDate.ToString($dateFormat)
} | ConvertTo-Json

Write-Host "Creating campaign (budget=100)..."
try {
    $campaign = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$BaseUrl/campaigns" `
        -ContentType "application/json" -Body $createBody
}
catch {
    Write-Host "ERROR: failed to create campaign: $_" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}

$campaignId = $campaign.id
if (-not $campaignId) {
    Write-Host "ERROR: create response had no 'id' field: $($campaign | ConvertTo-Json)" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}
Write-Host "Created campaign id=$campaignId"

# --- Fire concurrent impressions via hey ------------------------------------

$impressionUrl = "$BaseUrl/impression/$campaignId"
Write-Host "`nRunning hey: 2000 requests, 200 concurrent, POST $impressionUrl"

$heyOutput = & $HeyPath -n 2000 -c 200 -m POST $impressionUrl 2>&1 | Out-String
Write-Host $heyOutput

$statusCounts = @{}
foreach ($line in ($heyOutput -split "`n")) {
    if ($line -match '\[(\d{3})\]\s+(\d+)\s+responses') {
        $statusCounts[$matches[1]] = [int]$matches[2]
    }
}
$got200 = [int]($statusCounts["200"] | ForEach-Object { $_ } )
if (-not $got200) { $got200 = 0 }
$got409 = [int]($statusCounts["409"] | ForEach-Object { $_ } )
if (-not $got409) { $got409 = 0 }
$got500 = [int]($statusCounts["500"] | ForEach-Object { $_ } )
if (-not $got500) { $got500 = 0 }

Write-Host "hey status code distribution: 200=$got200 (expected 100), 409=$got409 (expected 1900), 500=$got500 (expected 0)"

# --- Check final stats -------------------------------------------------------

Write-Host "`nFetching GET /stats/$campaignId ..."
try {
    $stats = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Get -Uri "$BaseUrl/stats/$campaignId"
}
catch {
    Write-Host "ERROR: failed to fetch stats: $_" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}

$spentOk = ($stats.spent -eq 100)
$remainingOk = ($stats.remaining -eq 0)
$statusOk = ($stats.status -eq "paused")
$pass = $spentOk -and $remainingOk -and $statusOk

Write-Host ""
Write-Host "spent:     actual=$($stats.spent)     expected=100      $(if ($spentOk) { 'OK' } else { 'MISMATCH' })"
Write-Host "remaining: actual=$($stats.remaining)  expected=0        $(if ($remainingOk) { 'OK' } else { 'MISMATCH' })"
Write-Host "status:    actual=$($stats.status)  expected=paused   $(if ($statusOk) { 'OK' } else { 'MISMATCH' })"
Write-Host ""

if ($pass) {
    Write-Host "PASS" -ForegroundColor Green
    exit 0
}
else {
    Write-Host "FAIL" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}

- The budget must never go negative. This requirement is fixed. *

Mechanism: a single atomic conditional UPDATE (deducts and pauses in one statement, gated by a WHERE clause checking status/dates/remaining budget) — race-safe across multiple backend instances because Postgres evaluates the WHERE clause against the current row under lock as part of that one statement, not the application.

Bugs / incorrect behaviour** - `CampaignDetailPage.tsx:172-190` — the start/end date inputs are only `disabled={isCompleted}`. CLAUDE.md's own resolved decision says *"start_date/end_date can only be changed via PATCH while the campaign is paused; sending either while active or completed returns 409"* (line 54). So on an **active** campaign the form lets the user edit and submit new dates, guaranteeing a 409 round-trip that the code already knows about elsewhere (the same file goes out of its way, in `handleSave`, to avoid resending *unchanged* dates specifically because of this rule — see the comment at lines 116-120). The guard is applied to the "resend unchanged" case but not to the "active campaign" case. **2. CLAUDE.md rules not actually followed** - "Server state only through TanStack Query" (line 95) — `CampaignDetailPage.tsx:33,38-43` keeps `syncedCampaign`, a `useState` holding a full copy of the fetched `Campaign` object, purely so it can detect "a new object arrived from the query" and reset the form fields. That's server data duplicated into component state outside the query cache, which is exactly what this rule appears to rule out (even though the render-time-sync pattern itself is legitimate React). Everything else checked out: `types.ts` mirrors the API JSON exactly (including `remaining` being present, never separately stored/computed client-side); no `any` anywhere; money stays integer end-to-end (native `step=1`/`min=1` block non-integer submission); `CreateCampaignInput`/`UpdateCampaignInput` never include `id`/`status`/`spent`/timestamps; all server reads/writes go through `useQuery`/`useMutation`. **3. Dead code / debug output / inconsistent error handling / copy-paste drift** - `.btn-primary` is fully duplicated as a global (non-scoped) class in both `NewCampaignPage.css:44-52` and `CampaignDetailPage.css:71-80`, and the copies have drifted: the detail-page version adds `align-self: flex-start`, the new-campaign version doesn't. Since `router.tsx` eagerly imports all three page components, both stylesheets are bundled together, so which `align-self` value wins for `.btn-primary` anywhere in the app depends on CSS source order, not on either file read in isolation. `.btn-primary:disabled` is duplicated identically in both files too (harmless, but still copy-pasted rather than shared). - `CampaignDetailPage.tsx:288` — the "Send test impression" error is `

Sections, in this order:

1. What it is — two sentences.
2. Stack — one line each for backend, frontend, infra.
3. Running it — docker compose up from a clean clone, and the URL to open.

4. API — a table of all endpoints with their status codes.
5. Race condition — how it's solved (single conditional UPDATE, preconditions
   in the WHERE clause, auto-pause in the same statement), why not an
   in-process mutex, and how it's proven (Go concurrency test, hey load test,
   and the --scale backend=2 run). Leave a clearly marked placeholder where I
   will paste the load test output.
6. Decisions and why — one short paragraph each: whole TRY units with a single
   fixed currency; separate pause/resume/end endpoints instead of PATCH with a
   status field; no ?status= filter, the frontend filters client-side; soft
   delete returning 404 everywhere; spent is a lifetime counter, so the UI has
   "adjust budget by" rather than replacing the total; dates only editable
   while paused; the debug impression button is for demonstration only; one
   struct serves as DB row, domain object and API response.
7. Testing — what exists and what I prioritised.
8. Known limitations — migrations running on startup with multiple instances,
   budget accepting a quoted numeric string, no auth, no pagination, and the
   background completion job's up-to-60-second lag that produces the "Ended"
   label.
9. AI usage — two lines pointing at AI_CONTEXT.md, AI_WORKFLOW.md and
   ai_session/.

emoji, no decorative formatting. Don't invent features or endpoints — verify

content.content:
1	Claude Code did the implementation. I ran it in plan mode for anything non-trivial: it proposed a plan, I reviewed and approved or rejected it, then it wrote the code and I read the diff before committing.
2	
3	A Claude chat was used for one-off explanations: Go concepts I hadn't met before (why //go:embed can't reach a parent directory), and how TanStack Query's queries and mutations differ.
4	CLAUDE.md governed the implementation work. It's in the repo, and AI_CONTEXT.md explains how it was built and used.
5	
6	How the loop worked
7	
8	For every piece of work: decide what I wanted → plan mode → review the plan → implement → read the diff → verify by hand → commit → note anything that went wrong.
9	
10	The plan-before-code step is what made this work. Most of the problems below were caught in a plan, before they became code I'd have had to unpick.
11	
12	Where AI was wrong, and what I did
13	test suite that couldn't fail
14	
15	I asked for a backend test suite: no mocks, real Postgres, each test inside a transaction that's always rolled back so the shared dev database stays clean. That part worked — 14 rows before the run, 14 after, despite dozens of creates across the suite.
16	But partway through writing it, it produced this:
17	
18	go
19	func errorsAs(err error, target any) bool { return false }
20	
21	and wired it into an assertion checking that the result was false. That test would have passed unconditionally while proving nothing. In the same file it wrote var _ = strings.TrimSpace purely to silence an unused-import error instead of removing the import.
22	It caught and cleaned up both itself before anything ran, and the final code compiled and passed. But it changed how I think about generated tests: "all tests pass" means nothing until I've read the tests. I went back through the suite looking for assertions that couldn't fail, and concluded the suite was too large to review properly — around 1,100 lines for what the case study lists as a bonus item.
23	So I reverted it. The revert is in the commit history.
24	
25	A rule I never agreed to, shipped into the code
26	While planning PATCH, a plan stated as already-decided that campaign dates would only be editable while a campaign is paused. I hadn't decided that, and I said so explicitly and asked for it to be dropped.
27	It went into the code anyway, in both the service pre-check and the SQL WHERE clause. I only found it at the end, during a final read-only review pass over the whole backend, which flagged it as a CLAUDE.md rule the code didn't follow specifically against my own "do not decide open questions on your own" line. I kept the rule rather than removing it. dates affect whether impressions are accepted, so requiring a pause first is the safer behaviour, and pulling working backend logic out at the end of the project was the riskier choice.
28	
29	AI catching a contradiction in my own rules
30	
31	This one went the other way, and it is the best single piece of feedback I got.
32	
33	My CLAUDE.md said a database constraint violation is always a bug: return 500 and log it. Reviewing the file, Claude Code pointed out that this prejudges the concurrency decision I had deliberately left open, because one legitimate mechanism is to let the CHECK (spent <= budget) constraint reject the overspend, and in that design the violation is expected contention rather than a bug, and should be 409.
34	It was right. I reworded the rule with an explicit exception tied to whichever mechanism I chose. When I later chose the conditional UPDATE, a constraint violation genuinely did become a bug, and the rule was correct as written.
35	
36	Two bugs found by reading the code
37	
38	Both looked completely correct at a glance.
39	start_date and end_date weren't actually required. A missing date decodes to Go's zero time, 0001-01-01, which passes both "end after start" and "end is in the future". You could create a campaign starting in year 1. Fixed with an IsZero() check.
40	
41	The 200-character title limit used len(), which counts bytes, not characters. A Turkish title with several ş, ğ or ı would be wrongly rejected well short of 200 characters. Switched to utf8.RuneCountInString`
42	
43	The race condition
44	I deliberately left the mechanism undecided in CLAUDE.md, with an instruction to propose options and wait, specifically so I would get a real proposal rather than a rubber stamp on a decision I had already made.
45	It proposed four options.
46	
47	A, a single atomic conditional UPDATE. One statement does check and deduct together, with every precondition in the WHERE clause and the auto-pause in the same SET via `CASE WHEN spent + 1 >= budget`. Multi-instance correct, because Postgres locks the row and evaluates the whole WHERE clause against current committed state as one statement. Fewest round trips and shortest lock hold. The cost is that a failure is opaque, so it needs one follow-up SELECT to say why, paid only on failed requests.
48	
49	B, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside an explicit transaction. Also correct across instances, and the failure reason is known immediately with no extra read. The cost is two round trips on every call, with the row lock held across both plus any Go-side work in between, roughly double the lock hold time under contention.
50	
51	C, optimistic concurrency using compare-and-swap on `spent`. Correct, and no schema change, but under real contention on a single hot row most attempts lose and retry, which multiplies round trips. It suits low-contention fields; a hot campaign row is the opposite case.
52	
53	D, an in-process `sync.Mutex` per campaign id. Listed explicitly to rule out. Each instance has its own lock table, so two instances can each pass their own local check and both write. It works in single-instance testing and breaks silently the moment there is more than one instance.
54	
55	It also noted that a distributed lock, either a Postgres advisory lock or Redis, would work but only rebuilds with more moving parts the row-level serialization Postgres already provides, and Redis is out of scope in my CLAUDE.md anyway.
56	Was it good enough? Yes, and better than I expected on one specific point: it ruled out the mutex for the right reason, process-local state rather than vague robustness, and it named the real cost of option A rather than presenting it as free.
57	
58	I chose A. The guarantee has to survive the process, because the state lives in Postgres and not in Go. It is also the same idiom already used for the budget-decrease guard and the resume guard, so there is one concurrency story in the codebase instead of three. The ambiguity cost is real but paid only on failures, and the follow-up SELECT is used purely to choose an error message, never to decide whether the write happens, so it does not reintroduce a race. The write has already atomically succeeded or failed. Database CHECK constraints stay a pure safety net rather than the mechanism, which is what keeps "a constraint violation is a bug, return 500" meaningful.
59	
60	How much of the code did AI write
61	Most of it. I would estimate around 98% by line. Nearly all the Go and TypeScript was written by Claude Code from plans I approved.
62	What was mine: every design decision, including the data model, what "1 unit" means, the status transition rules, separate action endpoints instead of PATCH with a status field, a single fixed currency, and the concurrency mechanism. Rejecting plans, including a mock layer I didn't think earned its cost, an oversized test suite, the "VITE_API_BASE_URL" approach, and several proposed additions that were out of scope. Reviewing every diff, including the bugs above, which were caught by reading rather than by anything failing. And one full revert of AI-written code I couldn't vouch for.

file.content:
Claude Code did the implementation. I ran it in plan mode for anything non-trivial: it proposed a plan, I reviewed and approved or rejected it, then it wrote the code and I read the diff before committing.

A Claude chat was used for one-off explanations: Go concepts I hadn't met before (why //go:embed can't reach a parent directory), and how TanStack Query's queries and mutations differ.
CLAUDE.md governed the implementation work. It's in the repo, and AI_CONTEXT.md explains how it was built and used.

How the loop worked

For every piece of work: decide what I wanted → plan mode → review the plan → implement → read the diff → verify by hand → commit → note anything that went wrong.

The plan-before-code step is what made this work. Most of the problems below were caught in a plan, before they became code I'd have had to unpick.

Where AI was wrong, and what I did
test suite that couldn't fail

I asked for a backend test suite: no mocks, real Postgres, each test inside a transaction that's always rolled back so the shared dev database stays clean. That part worked — 14 rows before the run, 14 after, despite dozens of creates across the suite.
But partway through writing it, it produced this:

go
func errorsAs(err error, target any) bool { return false }

and wired it into an assertion checking that the result was false. That test would have passed unconditionally while proving nothing. In the same file it wrote var _ = strings.TrimSpace purely to silence an unused-import error instead of removing the import.
It caught and cleaned up both itself before anything ran, and the final code compiled and passed. But it changed how I think about generated tests: "all tests pass" means nothing until I've read the tests. I went back through the suite looking for assertions that couldn't fail, and concluded the suite was too large to review properly — around 1,100 lines for what the case study lists as a bonus item.
So I reverted it. The revert is in the commit history.

A rule I never agreed to, shipped into the code
While planning PATCH, a plan stated as already-decided that campaign dates would only be editable while a campaign is paused. I hadn't decided that, and I said so explicitly and asked for it to be dropped.
It went into the code anyway, in both the service pre-check and the SQL WHERE clause. I only found it at the end, during a final read-only review pass over the whole backend, which flagged it as a CLAUDE.md rule the code didn't follow specifically against my own "do not decide open questions on your own" line. I kept the rule rather than removing it. dates affect whether impressions are accepted, so requiring a pause first is the safer behaviour, and pulling working backend logic out at the end of the project was the riskier choice.

AI catching a contradiction in my own rules

This one went the other way, and it is the best single piece of feedback I got.

My CLAUDE.md said a database constraint violation is always a bug: return 500 and log it. Reviewing the file, Claude Code pointed out that this prejudges the concurrency decision I had deliberately left open, because one legitimate mechanism is to let the CHECK (spent <= budget) constraint reject the overspend, and in that design the violation is expected contention rather than a bug, and should be 409.
It was right. I reworded the rule with an explicit exception tied to whichever mechanism I chose. When I later chose the conditional UPDATE, a constraint violation genuinely did become a bug, and the rule was correct as written.

Two bugs found by reading the code

Both looked completely correct at a glance.
start_date and end_date weren't actually required. A missing date decodes to Go's zero time, 0001-01-01, which passes both "end after start" and "end is in the future". You could create a campaign starting in year 1. Fixed with an IsZero() check.

The 200-character title limit used len(), which counts bytes, not characters. A Turkish title with several ş, ğ or ı would be wrongly rejected well short of 200 characters. Switched to utf8.RuneCountInString`

The race condition
I deliberately left the mechanism undecided in CLAUDE.md, with an instruction to propose options and wait, specifically so I would get a real proposal rather than a rubber stamp on a decision I had already made.
It proposed four options.

A, a single atomic conditional UPDATE. One statement does check and deduct together, with every precondition in the WHERE clause and the auto-pause in the same SET via `CASE WHEN spent + 1 >= budget`. Multi-instance correct, because Postgres locks the row and evaluates the whole WHERE clause against current committed state as one statement. Fewest round trips and shortest lock hold. The cost is that a failure is opaque, so it needs one follow-up SELECT to say why, paid only on failed requests.

B, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside an explicit transaction. Also correct across instances, and the failure reason is known immediately with no extra read. The cost is two round trips on every call, with the row lock held across both plus any Go-side work in between, roughly double the lock hold time under contention.

C, optimistic concurrency using compare-and-swap on `spent`. Correct, and no schema change, but under real contention on a single hot row most attempts lose and retry, which multiplies round trips. It suits low-contention fields; a hot campaign row is the opposite case.

D, an in-process `sync.Mutex` per campaign id. Listed explicitly to rule out. Each instance has its own lock table, so two instances can each pass their own local check and both write. It works in single-instance testing and breaks silently the moment there is more than one instance.

It also noted that a distributed lock, either a Postgres advisory lock or Redis, would work but only rebuilds with more moving parts the row-level serialization Postgres already provides, and Redis is out of scope in my CLAUDE.md anyway.
Was it good enough? Yes, and better than I expected on one specific point: it ruled out the mutex for the right reason, process-local state rather than vague robustness, and it named the real cost of option A rather than presenting it as free.

I chose A. The guarantee has to survive the process, because the state lives in Postgres and not in Go. It is also the same idiom already used for the budget-decrease guard and the resume guard, so there is one concurrency story in the codebase instead of three. The ambiguity cost is real but paid only on failures, and the follow-up SELECT is used purely to choose an error message, never to decide whether the write happens, so it does not reintroduce a race. The write has already atomically succeeded or failed. Database CHECK constraints stay a pure safety net rather than the mechanism, which is what keeps "a constraint violation is a bug, return 500" meaningful.

How much of the code did AI write
Most of it. I would estimate around 98% by line. Nearly all the Go and TypeScript was written by Claude Code from plans I approved.
What was mine: every design decision, including the data model, what "1 unit" means, the status transition rules, separate action endpoints instead of PATCH with a status field, a single fixed currency, and the concurrency mechanism. Rejecting plans, including a mock layer I didn't think earned its cost, an oversized test suite, the "VITE_API_BASE_URL" approach, and several proposed additions that were out of scope. Reviewing every diff, including the bugs above, which were caught by reading rather than by anything failing. And one full revert of AI-written code I couldn't vouch for.

3	import (

21	)

23	func main() {
24		if err := run(); err != nil {
25			log.Fatal(err)
26		}
27	}
28	
29	func run() error {
30		databaseURL := os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")
31		if databaseURL == "" {
32			return errors.New("DATABASE_URL environment variable is required")
33		}
34	
35		port := os.Getenv("PORT")
36		if port == "" {
37			port = "8080"
38		}
39	
40		sweepInterval := time.Minute
41		if raw := os.Getenv("SWEEP_INTERVAL"); raw != "" {
42			parsed, err := time.ParseDuration(raw)
43			if err != nil {
44				return fmt.Errorf("parsing SWEEP_INTERVAL: %w", err)
45			}
46			sweepInterval = parsed
47		}
48	
49		if err := runMigrations(databaseURL); err != nil {
50			return fmt.Errorf("running migrations: %w", err)
51		}
52	
53		ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
54		defer stop()
55	
56		pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, databaseURL)
57		if err != nil {
58			return fmt.Errorf("creating pgxpool: %w", err)
59		}
60		defer pool.Close()
61	
62		repo := campaign.NewRepository(pool)
63		svc := campaign.NewService(repo)
64		h := campaign.NewHandler(svc)
65	
66		sweeper := campaign.NewSweeper(repo)
67		go sweeper.Run(ctx, sweepInterval)
68	
69		mux := http.NewServeMux()
70		mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns", h.Create)
71		mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns", h.List)
72		mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns/{id}", h.Get)
73		mux.HandleFunc("PATCH /campaigns/{id}", h.Update)
74		mux.HandleFunc("DELETE /campaigns/{id}", h.Delete)
75		mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns/{id}/pause", h.Pause)
76		mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns/{id}/resume", h.Resume)
77		mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns/{id}/end", h.End)
78		mux.HandleFunc("POST /impression/{id}", h.Impression)
79		mux.HandleFunc("GET /stats/{id}", h.Stats)
80	
81		server := &http.Server{
82			Addr:    ":" + port,
83			Handler: mux,
84		}
85	
86		errCh := make(chan error, 1)
87		go func() {
88			log.Printf("listening on :%s", port)
89			if err := server.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
90				errCh <- err
91			}
92		}()
93	
94		select {
95		case err := <-errCh:
96			return fmt.Errorf("server error: %w", err)
97		case <-ctx.Done():
98			log.Println("shutdown signal received")
99		}
100	
101		shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
102		defer cancel()
103		if err := server.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
104			return fmt.Errorf("server shutdown: %w", err)
105		}
106	
107		return nil
108	}

121		}
122	
123		if err := goose.Up(db, "."); err != nil {
124			return fmt.Errorf("goose up: %w", err)
125		}
126	
127		return nil
128	}

1	package campaign
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"time"
6	
7		"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
8	)
9	
10	type Repository struct {
11		pool *pgxpool.Pool
12	}
13	
14	func NewRepository(pool *pgxpool.Pool) *Repository {
15		return &Repository{pool: pool}
16	}
17	
18	const campaignColumns = "id, title, budget, spent, status, start_date, end_date, created_at, updated_at"
19	
20	func (r *Repository) Create(ctx context.Context, c Campaign) (Campaign, error) {
21		query := `
22			INSERT INTO campaigns (title, budget, start_date, end_date)
23			VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)
24			RETURNING ` + campaignColumns
25	
26		var out Campaign
27		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, c.Title, c.Budget, c.StartDate, c.EndDate).Scan(
28			&out.ID, &out.Title, &out.Budget, &out.Spent, &out.Status,
29			&out.StartDate, &out.EndDate, &out.CreatedAt, &out.UpdatedAt,
30		)
31		if err != nil {
32			return Campaign{}, err
33		}
34		return out, nil
35	}
36	
37	func (r *Repository) List(ctx context.Context) ([]Campaign, error) {
38		query := `
39			SELECT ` + campaignColumns + `
40			FROM campaigns
41			WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
42			ORDER BY created_at DESC`
43	
44		rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx, query)
45		if err != nil {
46			return nil, err
47		}
48		defer rows.Close()
49	
50		campaigns := []Campaign{} // non-nil so a zero-row result marshals to [] not null
51		for rows.Next() {
52			var c Campaign
53			if err := rows.Scan(
54				&c.ID, &c.Title, &c.Budget, &c.Spent, &c.Status,
55				&c.StartDate, &c.EndDate, &c.CreatedAt, &c.UpdatedAt,
56			); err != nil {
57				return nil, err
58			}
59			campaigns = append(campaigns, c)
60		}
61		if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
62			return nil, err
63		}
64		return campaigns, nil
65	}
66	
67	func (r *Repository) GetByID(ctx context.Context, id int64) (Campaign, error) {
68		query := `
69			SELECT ` + campaignColumns + `
70			FROM campaigns
71			WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`
72	
73		var c Campaign
74		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id).Scan(
75			&c.ID, &c.Title, &c.Budget, &c.Spent, &c.Status,
76			&c.StartDate, &c.EndDate, &c.CreatedAt, &c.UpdatedAt,
77		)
78		if err != nil {
79			return Campaign{}, err
80		}
81		return c, nil
82	}
83	
84	// Update applies a partial update, using COALESCE so an absent (nil) field
85	// keeps the column's current value. Both invariants below are enforced as
86	// WHERE conditions rather than checked beforehand in Go, so they're evaluated
87	// by Postgres atomically against the current row under lock as part of this
88	// single statement — race-safe across multiple backend instances without any
89	// extra locking on our side:
90	//   - spent <= COALESCE(budget, budget): a no-op when budget isn't being
91	//     changed (spent <= budget already holds via the CHECK constraint), and
92	//     the real budget-decrease-vs-spent guard when it is.
93	//   - dates only touchable while paused: vacuously true when neither date
94	//     param is set, otherwise requires status = 'paused'.
95	//
96	// Zero matching rows surfaces as pgx.ErrNoRows via Scan, same as GetByID.
97	func (r *Repository) Update(ctx context.Context, id int64, title *string, budget *int64, startDate, endDate *time.Time) (Campaign, error) {
98		// Params are explicitly cast (::text/::bigint/::timestamptz) because when
99		// every optional field but one is nil, Postgres can't always infer a
100		// placeholder's type from COALESCE/IS NULL context alone and rejects the
101		// query with "could not determine data type of parameter" (42P08).
102		query := `
103			UPDATE campaigns
104			SET
105				title      = COALESCE($2::text, title),
106				budget     = COALESCE($3::bigint, budget),
107				start_date = COALESCE($4::timestamptz, start_date),
108				end_date   = COALESCE($5::timestamptz, end_date),
109				updated_at = now()
110			WHERE id = $1
111				AND deleted_at IS NULL
112				AND status <> 'completed'
113				AND spent <= COALESCE($3::bigint, budget)
114				AND (($4::timestamptz IS NULL AND $5::timestamptz IS NULL) OR status = 'paused')
115			RETURNING ` + campaignColumns
116	
117		var out Campaign
118		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id, title, budget, startDate, endDate).Scan(
119			&out.ID, &out.Title, &out.Budget, &out.Spent, &out.Status,
120			&out.StartDate, &out.EndDate, &out.CreatedAt, &out.UpdatedAt,
121		)
122		if err != nil {
123			return Campaign{}, err
124		}
125		return out, nil
126	}
127	
128	// SoftDelete never issues a DELETE statement — it sets deleted_at, and every
129	// query elsewhere filters deleted_at IS NULL. No status restriction: any
130	// non-deleted campaign, regardless of status, can be soft-deleted.
131	func (r *Repository) SoftDelete(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
132		query := `
133			UPDATE campaigns
134			SET deleted_at = now(), updated_at = now()
135			WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL
136			RETURNING id`
137	
138		var returnedID int64
139		return r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id).Scan(&returnedID)
140	}
141	
142	// Pause is the same conditional-UPDATE idiom as Update/Deduct: the WHERE
143	// clause is the sole enforcement mechanism, so zero matching rows surfaces
144	// as pgx.ErrNoRows and gets disambiguated by classifyUpdateConflict.
145	func (r *Repository) Pause(ctx context.Context, id int64) (Campaign, error) {
146		query := `
147			UPDATE campaigns
148			SET status = 'paused', updated_at = now()
149			WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL AND status = 'active'
150			RETURNING ` + campaignColumns
151	
152		var out Campaign
153		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id).Scan(
154			&out.ID, &out.Title, &out.Budget, &out.Spent, &out.Status,
155			&out.StartDate, &out.EndDate, &out.CreatedAt, &out.UpdatedAt,
156		)
157		if err != nil {
158			return Campaign{}, err
159		}
160		return out, nil
161	}
162	
163	// Resume: spent < budget and end_date > now() are evaluated by Postgres
164	// atomically against the current row as part of this one statement, so a
165	// concurrent impression exhausting the budget at the same instant can't
166	// race past this check — whichever statement runs first wins, and the other
167	// correctly sees the post-write state.
168	func (r *Repository) Resume(ctx context.Context, id int64) (Campaign, error) {
169		query := `
170			UPDATE campaigns
171			SET status = 'active', updated_at = now()
172			WHERE id = $1
173				AND deleted_at IS NULL
174				AND status = 'paused'
175				AND spent < budget
176				AND end_date > now()
177			RETURNING ` + campaignColumns
178	
179		var out Campaign
180		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id).Scan(
181			&out.ID, &out.Title, &out.Budget, &out.Spent, &out.Status,
182			&out.StartDate, &out.EndDate, &out.CreatedAt, &out.UpdatedAt,
183		)
184		if err != nil {
185			return Campaign{}, err
186		}
187		return out, nil
188	}
189	
190	// End works from either 'active' or 'paused' — only 'completed' blocks it.
191	func (r *Repository) End(ctx context.Context, id int64) (Campaign, error) {
192		query := `
193			UPDATE campaigns
194			SET status = 'completed', updated_at = now()
195			WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL AND status <> 'completed'
196			RETURNING ` + campaignColumns
197	
198		var out Campaign
199		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id).Scan(
200			&out.ID, &out.Title, &out.Budget, &out.Spent, &out.Status,
201			&out.StartDate, &out.EndDate, &out.CreatedAt, &out.UpdatedAt,
202		)
203		if err != nil {
204			return Campaign{}, err
205		}
206		return out, nil
207	}
208	
209	// CompletePastEndDate marks every active/paused campaign whose end_date has
210	// passed as completed. This is a catch-up sweep, not a correctness
211	// mechanism — Deduct and Resume already check dates themselves — so a
212	// missed or delayed sweep can't let an impression through past end_date.
213	func (r *Repository) CompletePastEndDate(ctx context.Context) (int64, error) {
214		query := `
215			UPDATE campaigns
216			SET status = 'completed', updated_at = now()
217			WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
218				AND status IN ('active', 'paused')
219				AND end_date <= now()`
220	
221		tag, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, query)
222		if err != nil {
223			return 0, err
224		}
225		return tag.RowsAffected(), nil
226	}
227	
228	// Deduct atomically records one impression: increments spent by 1 and, if
229	// this deduction exhausts the budget, flips status to 'paused' in the same
230	// statement — no separate transition step, so no window where a concurrent
231	// call could sneak in between "deduct" and "pause". The WHERE clause is the
232	// sole correctness mechanism, evaluated by Postgres against the current row
233	// under lock as part of this one statement, so it's race-safe across
234	// multiple backend instances without any extra locking on our side.
235	func (r *Repository) Deduct(ctx context.Context, id int64) (Campaign, error) {
236		query := `
237			UPDATE campaigns
238			SET
239				spent  = spent + 1,
240				status = CASE WHEN spent + 1 >= budget THEN 'paused' ELSE status END,
241				updated_at = now()
242			WHERE id = $1
243				AND deleted_at IS NULL
244				AND status = 'active'
245				AND start_date <= now()
246				AND end_date > now()
247				AND spent < budget
248			RETURNING ` + campaignColumns
249	
250		var out Campaign
251		err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, query, id).Scan(
252			&out.ID, &out.Title, &out.Budget, &out.Spent, &out.Status,
253			&out.StartDate, &out.EndDate, &out.CreatedAt, &out.UpdatedAt,
254		)
255		if err != nil {
256			return Campaign{}, err
257		}
258		return out, nil
259	}
260

27	// stored (budget - spent), so it's derived here rather than on the struct.
28	func (c Campaign) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
29		type Alias Campaign // defined type, not an alias — drops MarshalJSON so this doesn't recurse
30	
31		// pgx returns scanned timestamps in the driver/host's local Location; the
32		// instant is correct but json's RFC3339 output would print that offset
33		// instead of "Z". Normalize to UTC here so every response is UTC.
34		c.StartDate = c.StartDate.UTC()
35		c.EndDate = c.EndDate.UTC()
36		c.CreatedAt = c.CreatedAt.UTC()
37		c.UpdatedAt = c.UpdatedAt.UTC()
38	
39		return json.Marshal(struct {
40			Alias
41			Remaining int64 `json:"remaining"`
42		}{
43			Alias:     Alias(c),
44			Remaining: c.Budget - c.Spent,
45		})
46	}

56	// "field sent" — required for PATCH's partial-update semantics.
57	type UpdateInput struct {
58		Title     *string      `json:"title"`
59		Budget    *json.Number `json:"budget"`
60		StartDate *time.Time   `json:"start_date"`
61		EndDate   *time.Time   `json:"end_date"`
62	}

67		Spent       int64  `json:"spent"`
68		Remaining   int64  `json:"remaining"`
69		Budget      int64  `json:"budget"`
70		Status      string `json:"status"`
71	}
72

74	// separate counter, since 1 impression always equals 1 unit spent.
75	func (c Campaign) Stats() Stats {

77			Impressions: c.Spent,
78			Spent:       c.Spent,
79			Remaining:   c.Budget - c.Spent,
80			Budget:      c.Budget,
81			Status:      c.Status,

18	// TestConcurrentImpressions_NeverOverspend proves the Definition of Done
19	// requirement: under heavy concurrent load against a single campaign, spent
20	// never exceeds budget. It runs against the real Postgres started by
21	// docker compose, per CLAUDE.md's testing approach (no mocks).
22	func TestConcurrentImpressions_NeverOverspend(t *testing.T) {
23		databaseURL := os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")
24		if databaseURL == "" {
25			t.Skip("DATABASE_URL not set; run against the Postgres started by docker compose")
26		}
27	
28		ctx := context.Background()
29		pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, databaseURL)
30		if err != nil {
31			t.Fatalf("connecting to database: %v", err)
32		}
33		defer pool.Close()
34	
35		repo := campaign.NewRepository(pool)
36		svc := campaign.NewService(repo)
37	
38		const budget = 50
39		const concurrency = 300
40	
41		created, err := svc.Create(ctx, campaign.CreateInput{
42			Title:     "concurrency test",
43			Budget:    json.Number(strconv.Itoa(budget)),
44			StartDate: time.Now().Add(-time.Hour),
45			EndDate:   time.Now().Add(time.Hour),
46		})
47		if err != nil {
48			t.Fatalf("creating test campaign: %v", err)
49		}
50		t.Cleanup(func() {
51			_ = svc.Delete(context.Background(), created.ID)
52		})
53	
54		var successes int64
55		var wg sync.WaitGroup
56		wg.Add(concurrency)
57		for i := 0; i < concurrency; i++ {
58			go func() {
59				defer wg.Done()
60				if _, err := svc.RecordImpression(ctx, created.ID); err == nil {
61					atomic.AddInt64(&successes, 1)
62				}
63			}()
64		}
65		wg.Wait()
66	
67		if successes != budget {
68			t.Fatalf("expected exactly %d successful impressions, got %d", budget, successes)
69		}
70	
71		final, err := svc.Get(ctx, created.ID)
72		if err != nil {
73			t.Fatalf("fetching final campaign state: %v", err)
74		}
75		if final.Spent != budget {
76			t.Fatalf("expected spent == %d, got %d", budget, final.Spent)
77		}
78		if final.Spent > final.Budget {
79			t.Fatalf("budget went negative: spent=%d budget=%d", final.Spent, final.Budget)
80		}
81		if final.Status != campaign.StatusPaused {
82			t.Fatalf("expected status %q after exhausting budget, got %q", campaign.StatusPaused, final.Status)
83		}
84	}

17	// completed") actually flips status, and leaves campaigns still within
18	// their window untouched. It's a catch-up/cosmetic job, not a correctness
19	// mechanism, so this exercises the repository method the sweeper calls
20	// directly rather than waiting out a real ticker interval.
21	func TestSweeper_CompletesPastEndDate(t *testing.T) {
22		databaseURL := os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")
23		if databaseURL == "" {
24			t.Skip("DATABASE_URL not set; run against the Postgres started by docker compose")
25		}
26	
27		ctx := context.Background()
28		pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, databaseURL)
29		if err != nil {
30			t.Fatalf("connecting to database: %v", err)
31		}
32		defer pool.Close()
33	
34		repo := campaign.NewRepository(pool)
35		svc := campaign.NewService(repo)
36	
37		// Created with a valid (future) end_date, since Create rejects a past
38		// one, then backdated directly in SQL to simulate a campaign whose
39		// window has since elapsed.
40		expired, err := svc.Create(ctx, campaign.CreateInput{
41			Title:     "sweeper test - expired",
42			Budget:    json.Number("100"),
43			StartDate: time.Now().Add(-2 * time.Hour),
44			EndDate:   time.Now().Add(time.Hour),
45		})
46		if err != nil {
47			t.Fatalf("creating expired test campaign: %v", err)
48		}
49		t.Cleanup(func() { _ = svc.Delete(context.Background(), expired.ID) })
50	
51		if _, err := pool.Exec(ctx, `UPDATE campaigns SET end_date = $1 WHERE id = $2`,
52			time.Now().Add(-time.Minute), expired.ID); err != nil {
53			t.Fatalf("backdating end_date: %v", err)
54		}
55	
56		current, err := svc.Create(ctx, campaign.CreateInput{
57			Title:     "sweeper test - current",
58			Budget:    json.Number("100"),
59			StartDate: time.Now().Add(-time.Hour),
60			EndDate:   time.Now().Add(time.Hour),
61		})
62		if err != nil {
63			t.Fatalf("creating current test campaign: %v", err)
64		}
65		t.Cleanup(func() { _ = svc.Delete(context.Background(), current.ID) })
66	
67		if _, err := repo.CompletePastEndDate(ctx); err != nil {
68			t.Fatalf("sweeping: %v", err)
69		}
70	
71		swept, err := svc.Get(ctx, expired.ID)
72		if err != nil {
73			t.Fatalf("fetching expired campaign: %v", err)
74		}
75		if swept.Status != campaign.StatusCompleted {
76			t.Fatalf("expected expired campaign to be completed, got %q", swept.Status)
77		}
78		if !swept.UpdatedAt.After(expired.UpdatedAt) {
79			t.Fatalf("expected updated_at to advance after sweep")
80		}
81	
82		untouched, err := svc.Get(ctx, current.ID)
83		if err != nil {
84			t.Fatalf("fetching current campaign: %v", err)
85		}
86		if untouched.Status != campaign.StatusActive {
87			t.Fatalf("expected current campaign to remain active, got %q", untouched.Status)
88		}

# Mini-Ad-Campaign

## What it is

Mini-Ad-Campaign is a minimal platform for a retailer to manage ad campaigns and record impressions against a fixed budget. Each impression deducts one unit from the campaign's budget, and a campaign pauses itself the instant that budget is exhausted.

## Stack

Backend: Go 1.27, HTTP via the standard `net/http`, Postgres via `pgx`/`pgxpool`, schema migrations via goose (embedded into the binary and run on startup).

Frontend: React + TypeScript on Vite, server state via TanStack Query, plain CSS, client-side routing via `react-router`.

Infra: Docker Compose runs three services — Postgres, the Go backend (no published port; reachable only inside the compose network), and nginx, which serves the built frontend and proxies `/api/` to the backend.

## Running it

With Docker Compose, from a clean clone:

```

The campaign detail page exposes "adjust budget by" (a delta) rather than a field that replaces the total, because replacing it would invite typing a new absolute number without the current spend in view, and a decrease is only valid down to `spent` at write time — which is exactly what the underlying WHERE-clause guard enforces.

`start_date`/`end_date` can only be changed via `PATCH` while the campaign is paused; sending either while active or completed returns 409, enforced both in the service and in the `UPDATE`'s WHERE clause. Dates gate whether impressions are accepted at all, so letting them change underneath a campaign that's actively serving impressions would let a single edit silently start or stop deduction — the same class of problem the budget guards exist to prevent.

The campaign detail page has a "Send test impression" button under a section labelled "Debug / Simulation." In production, impressions are recorded by whatever ad server serves the creative, not by a person clicking a button; the control exists only so the deduction and auto-pause behavior can be seen working from the UI without a separate HTTP client.

`Campaign` (`backend/internal/campaign/campaign.go`) is scanned directly from Postgres rows, passed around as the domain type, and marshalled directly as the API response, with a computed `remaining` field added via a custom `MarshalJSON` since remaining is never stored. Three responsibilities on one struct is a coupling that would matter once the wire shape and the storage shape needed to evolve independently; at this size, three structs to keep hand-synced would be its own source of bugs, and there is currently nowhere they'd need to diverge.

## Testing

The backend has two Go test files, both run against the real Postgres started by Docker Compose rather than a mock (`DATABASE_URL` unset skips them, so a bare `go test ./...` without Postgres running doesn't fail). `impression_test.go` fires 300 concurrent impressions at a single campaign and asserts the budget invariant end-to-end, in-process. `sweeper_test.go` asserts the background job flips a past-end-date campaign to completed and leaves a current one untouched. `loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1` extends the same assertion over real HTTP and across multiple backend instances, as described above.

Coverage was kept small and directly readable rather than broad. An earlier, AI-generated backend test suite (roughly 1,100 lines) was reverted after a read turned up an assertion that could never fail — see `ai_sessions/AI_WORKFLOW.md`. The priority since has been proving the one invariant that's a hard rule — the budget never goes negative, under real concurrency, over real HTTP, across multiple instances — over maximizing line coverage. The frontend has no automated tests.

## Known limitations

Each backend instance runs its own database migrations on startup (`goose.Up` inside `main.go`'s `run()`) before it starts serving. With a single instance this is fine; with `docker compose up -d --scale backend=2`, or any multi-instance deployment, every instance attempts the same migration run concurrently on startup, and correctness there depends on goose and Postgres serializing that safely rather than on anything this codebase does deliberately.

`budget` is decoded as `json.Number`, which accepts both a bare JSON number (`100`) and a quoted numeric string (`"100"`). This is intentional laxness rather than a validation gap — a non-numeric value still fails with 400, and the frontend never sends budget as a string — but the field is looser about its JSON type than the rest of the schema.

There is no authentication or authorization anywhere in the API. Any client that can reach the backend can create, edit, pause, resume, end, delete, or record impressions against any campaign; this is explicitly out of scope, not an oversight.

`GET /campaigns` returns every non-deleted campaign in a single response, with no pagination. That's fine at the scale a single retailer's campaign list actually reaches, and would need revisiting before it could serve a materially larger dataset.

The background sweep that marks past-end-date campaigns completed is a cosmetic catch-up job, not a correctness mechanism — impressions and resumes check dates themselves regardless of stored status. In local development it runs on `SWEEP_INTERVAL` (default `1m`), so the stored `status` can lag up to a minute behind a campaign's actual end date. Under `docker compose up`, this currently runs far more often than intended: `docker-compose.yml` interpolates `SWEEP_INTERVAL` as `${SWEEP_INTERVAL:-1m}s`, and with `.env`'s `SWEEP_INTERVAL=1m` that produces the literal duration string `1ms`, not one minute, which was confirmed with `docker compose config`. The frontend's `displayStatus()` (`frontend/src/lib/status.ts`) computes an `Ended` label from the dates directly, so the UI never shows a stale "Active"/"Paused" badge either way, but anything reading the API's raw `status` field can see it lag behind the true end date until the next sweep.

75	## Race condition
76	
77	The impression endpoint accepts hundreds of concurrent requests against the same campaign, and the budget must never go negative. This is enforced with a single atomic conditional UPDATE (`Repository.Deduct` in `backend/internal/campaign/repository.go`): one SQL statement increments `spent` by 1 and, in the same `SET`, via `CASE WHEN spent + 1 >= budget THEN 'paused' ELSE status END`, flips the campaign to paused if that increment exhausts the budget. Every precondition — active, started, not ended, budget remaining — sits in the `WHERE` clause rather than in Go. Postgres evaluates that whole `WHERE` clause against the current committed row under lock as part of the one statement, so there is no window between checking and writing, regardless of how many separate backend processes are issuing the statement at once. If zero rows match, nothing is written, and the service issues one follow-up `SELECT` purely to work out which precondition failed and choose a 409 message — that read never decides whether the write happens, so it cannot reintroduce a race. 80	
81	This is proven at three levels. `backend/internal/campaign/impression_test.go` (`TestConcurrentImpressions_NeverOverspend`) fires 300 concurrent goroutines at a budget-50 campaign inside a single process and asserts exactly 50 succeed, `spent == budget`, and the campaign ends up paused. `loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1` repeats the same assertion over real HTTP: it creates a budget-100 campaign, fires 2000 concurrent `POST /impression/{id}` requests at it with `hey`, and checks `GET /stats/{id}` for `spent == 100`, `remaining == 0`, `status == paused`. 87	```

90	
91	The backend has two Go test files, both run against the real Postgres started by Docker Compose rather than a mock (`DATABASE_URL` unset skips them, so a bare `go test ./...` without Postgres running doesn't fail). `impression_test.go` fires 300 concurrent impressions at a single campaign and asserts the budget invariant end-to-end, in-process. `sweeper_test.go` asserts the background job flips a past-end-date campaign to completed and leaves a current one untouched. `loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1` extends the same assertion over real HTTP and across multiple backend instances, as described above.
92	
93	Coverage was kept small and directly readable rather than broad. An earlier, AI-generated backend test suite (roughly 1,100 lines) was reverted after a read turned up an assertion that could never fail — see `ai_sessions/AI_WORKFLOW.md`. The priority since has been proving the one invariant that's a hard rule — the budget never goes negative, under real concurrency, over real HTTP, across multiple instances — over maximizing line coverage. The frontend has no automated tests.
94	
95	## Known limitations
96	
97	Each backend instance runs its own database migrations on startup (`goose.Up` inside `main.go`'s `run()`) before it starts serving; with `docker compose up -d --scale backend=2`, or any multi-instance deployment, every instance attempts the same migration run concurrently on startup, and correctness there, goose takes an advisory lock for this, but I haven't verified the behaviour under simultaneous startup
98	
99	`budget` is decoded as `json.Number`, which accepts both a bare JSON number (`100`) and a quoted numeric string (`"100"`). This is intentional laxness rather than a validation gap.
100	
101	The background sweep that marks past-end-date campaigns completed is a cosmetic catch-up job, not a correctness mechanism — impressions and resumes check dates themselves regardless of stored status. It runs on `SWEEP_INTERVAL` (default `1m`, in both local development and under `docker compose up`), so the stored `status` can lag up to a minute behind a campaign's actual end date. The frontend's `displayStatus()` (`frontend/src/lib/status.ts`) computes an `Ended` label from the dates directly, so the UI never shows a stale "Active"/"Paused" badge either way, but anything reading the API's raw `status` field can see it lag behind the true end date until the next sweep.

# Mini-Ad-Campaign

## What it is

Mini-Ad-Campaign is a minimal platform for a retailer to manage ad campaigns and record impressions against a fixed budget. Each impression deducts one unit from the campaign's budget, and a campaign pauses itself the instant that budget is exhausted.

## Stack

Backend: Go 1.27, HTTP via the standard `net/http`, Postgres via `pgx`/`pgxpool`, schema migrations via goose (embedded into the binary and run on startup).

Frontend: React + TypeScript on Vite, server state via TanStack Query, plain CSS, client-side routing via `react-router`.

Infra: Docker Compose runs three services — Postgres, the Go backend (no published port; reachable only inside the compose network), and nginx, which serves the built frontend and proxies `/api/` to the backend.

## Running it

With Docker Compose, from a clean clone:

```
docker compose up
```

Open http://localhost:3000. nginx serves the frontend there and proxies `/api/*` through to the backend.

### Local development

Start only Postgres via Compose:

```
docker compose up -d postgres
```

Backend (from `backend/`), pointed at that Postgres instance:

PowerShell:
```
$env:DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable"
go run ./cmd/server
```

bash:
```
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable"
go run ./cmd/server
```

The server listens on `:8080` by default (`PORT`) and runs its own migrations against `DATABASE_URL` on startup.

Frontend (from `frontend/`), the same in either shell:

```
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:5173. Vite proxies `/api/*` to `http://localhost:8080` (see `vite.config.ts`), so the backend above needs to be running on port 8080 for this to work.

## API

| Method | Path | Description | Success | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| POST | /campaigns | Create a campaign | 201 | 400 |
| GET | /campaigns | List campaigns, excluding soft-deleted, newest first | 200 | |
| GET | /campaigns/{id} | Get one campaign | 200 | 404 |

| POST | /campaigns/{id}/resume | paused to active | 200 | 404, 409 |
| POST | /campaigns/{id}/end | active or paused to completed | 200 | 404, 409 |
| POST | /impression/{id} | Record one impression; deducts one budget unit | 200 | 404, 409 |
| GET | /stats/{id} | impressions, spent, remaining, budget, status | 200 | 404 |

Every endpoint above also returns 400 if `{id}` isn't a valid integer, and 500 with `{"error": "internal server error"}` on an unexpected failure.

## Race condition

The impression endpoint accepts hundreds of concurrent requests against the same campaign, and the budget must never go negative. This is enforced with a single atomic conditional UPDATE (`Repository.Deduct` in `backend/internal/campaign/repository.go`): one SQL statement increments `spent` by 1 and, in the same `SET`, via `CASE WHEN spent + 1 >= budget THEN 'paused' ELSE status END`, flips the campaign to paused if that increment exhausts the budget. Each additional backend instance would carry its own independent lock table, so two instances could each pass their own local check and both write — correct under single-instance testing, and silently broken the moment there is more than one instance, which is exactly the failure Postgres's row-level locking rules out without any extra machinery on the application side.

The frontend has no automated tests.

## Known limitations

Each backend instance runs its own database migrations on startup (`goose.Up` inside `main.go`'s `run()`) before it starts serving; with `docker compose up -d --scale backend=2`, or any multi-instance deployment, every instance attempts the same migration run concurrently on startup, and correctness there, goose takes an advisory lock for this, but I haven't verified the behaviour under simultaneous startup

`budget` is decoded as `json.Number`, which accepts both a bare JSON number (`100`) and a quoted numeric string (`"100"`). This is intentional laxness rather than a validation gap.

The background sweep that marks past-end-date campaigns completed is a cosmetic catch-up job, not a correctness mechanism — impressions and resumes check dates themselves regardless of stored status. It runs on `SWEEP_INTERVAL` (default `1m`, in both local development and under `docker compose up`), so the stored `status` can lag up to a minute behind a campaign's actual end date. The frontend's `displayStatus()` (`frontend/src/lib/status.ts`) computes an `Ended` label from the dates directly, so the UI never shows a stale "Active"/"Paused" badge either way, but anything reading the API's raw `status` field can see it lag behind the true end date until the next sweep.

This is enforced with a single atomic conditional UPDATE (`Repository.Deduct` in `backend/internal/campaign/repository.go`): one SQL statement increments `spent` by 1 and, in the same `SET`, via `CASE WHEN spent + 1 >= budget THEN 'paused' ELSE status END`, flips the campaign to paused if that increment exhausts the budget. Every precondition — active, started, not ended, budget remaining — sits in the `WHERE` clause rather than in Go. Postgres evaluates that whole `WHERE` clause against the current committed row under lock as part of the one statement, so there is no window between checking and writing, regardless of how many separate backend processes are issuing the statement at once. An in-process mutex was considered and rejected. A `sync.Mutex`, or any per-process lock, only serializes goroutines inside one Go process's memory; it cannot see what another process is doing. Each additional backend instance would carry its own independent lock table, so two instances could each pass their own local check and both write — correct under single-instance testing, and silently broken the moment there is more than one instance, which is exactly the failure Postgres's row-level locking rules out without any extra machinery on the application side.

This is proven at three levels. `backend/internal/campaign/impression_test.go` (`TestConcurrentImpressions_NeverOverspend`) fires 300 concurrent goroutines at a budget-50 campaign inside a single process and asserts exactly 50 succeed, `spent == budget`, and the campaign ends up paused. `loadtest/budget-loadtest.ps1` repeats the same assertion over real HTTP: it creates a budget-100 campaign, fires 2000 concurrent `POST /impression/{id}` requests at it with `hey`, and checks `GET /stats/{id}` for `spent == 100`, `remaining == 0`, `status == paused`. Finally, that same load test is re-run against `docker compose up -d --scale backend=2` through nginx — two separate backend processes sharing one Postgres instance — which is the scenario an in-process mutex cannot survive but the conditional UPDATE can.
